## Introduction

In a recent episode of the [Software Engineering
Radio](https://www.se-radio.net/) podcast, I interviewed [Dave
Airlie](https://airlied.blogspot.com/), a distinguished engineer at [Red
Hat](https://www.redhat.com/) and a longtime Linux kernel maintainer who leads
the Direct Rendering Manager (DRM) subsystem, which provides graphics and GPU
support. Our conversation explored what it takes to maintain a subsystem that
receives over 300 contributors in a single kernel release, how the
[nine-to-ten-week kernel release
cycle](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/process/2.Process.html) actually
works, and why the standard response to a regression is to revert first and ask
questions later. Dave is also candid about the limits of vendor code sharing
across operating systems, warning that in his experience it "generally doesn't
end with Linux being better off." He closes by explaining why he supports
bringing Rust into the kernel and how AI-assisted review is starting to help
with a chronic reviewer shortage. As a long-time Linux enthusiast, I'm thankful
that Dave took the time for this interview.

## Insights

Before you listen to the full episode, please check out some of its insights:

**What is the scale of the Linux kernel and of the DRM subsystem?**

Dave describes the size of the project he helps to maintain:

> "Linux kernel is, well, we consider it's probably the biggest software
> engineering project in the world, at least that's what we like to say. In
> terms of maintainers, the number is varied. Changeable, I would say on average
> is between 80, a 100, 150."

He also shares a number that surprised him when he checked it:

> "If you'd asked me this yesterday, I would've said a hundred, but I ran the
> numbers last night and apparently, we have over 300 people contributing every
> kernel release to the DRM subsystem, which actually surprised me just as
> much."

**How does the kernel's release cycle work?**

Dave walks through the merge window and the release candidates that follow it:

> "overall on the kernel has what we call a nine-to-10-week release cycle. ...
> The way that works is the first two weeks of every new kernel development
> cycle are called the merge window. That's where Linus takes all of the pull
> requests from all of the others, all of the maintainers under him and he puts
> them all together and stabilizes that for two weeks. And we hope in those two
> weeks that that's a runnable kernel. At the end of that two weeks, he'll
> release what's called RC1 and then on a weekly basis, usually on a Sunday
> afternoon Pacific time, he will release RC2, RC3 up until RC7 usually, and
> then from RC7 he will release the final one the following week."

**What counts as a regression, and how do maintainers respond to one?**

Dave defines a regression and explains the discipline that follows from it:

> "regression is made to be something that broke in RC1, if something is merged
> during RC1 that causes anything to go be worse than it was before RC1, then
> it's considered a regression. The standard method of dealing with regressions
> is to revert first ask questions later. ... So we should remove the patch that
> caused the problem and then work out what the problem was and fix it in the
> next cycle."

He adds that a regression only becomes urgent when somebody notices the
problem:

> "if it made something worse for a user, whether that user is causing a
> performance difference or that user is seeing a functional break in their
> hardware. ... If a regression happens and nobody notices, it's not considered
> a regression till someone notices."

**How is AI changing the review of kernel patches?**

Dave describes how a colleague at Meta built a regression detector and
evaluated it against the project's own history:

> "I talked to a guy called Chris Mason at Meta has been leading their work on
> this. He actually wrote framework for regression finding, for using AI. So, it
> was very specifically focused on prompting AI to sort of find regressions. And
> how he tested it was by running it on older kernel patches and then finding
> fixes for those older kernel patches."

He argues that even an imperfect reviewer is worth having, because the cost of a
regression is so high:

> "Even if there's noise in that system, it's still better. ... when that
> regression actually gets into the Linux kernel and gets out into the world
> that costs like actual money in the world."

**Why do you support bringing Rust into the Linux kernel?**

Dave explains that his motivation has as much to do with people as with
programming languages:

> "My push for getting behind the Rust effort was actually more social and
> community focused. ... one of the big complaints in the private meeting over
> the years as we're all getting older. There's, we've got a lot more gray
> beards, like people are in their fifties now that were in their twenties when
> they started this journey."

He also expects Rust to reduce a particular class of mistakes that kernel
developers keep repeating:

> "I see Rust accelerating the ability to deliver GPU drivers. I see it being
> much faster that we can build a lot more common infrastructure. We can avoid
> making a lot of the C mistakes that we've repeatedly made. ... lifetimes are
> one of the hardest things to get right in the Linux kernel."
